name: PgQueuer
summary: A Python background-job library that uses Postgres as the broker: `SKIP LOCKED` to claim, LISTEN/NOTIFY to wake.
intro: PgQueuer is a Python library that turns a Postgres database into a job queue. `pgq install` creates a `pgqueuer` table, a log table and a trigger. A producer calls `queries.enqueue(entrypoint, payload)`, which inserts a row, and the trigger sends a `NOTIFY` that wakes listening workers. A worker, started with `pgq run module:factory`, claims up to `batch_size` ready rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, marks them `picked` and runs the async handler registered for that entrypoint. While a job runs, the worker refreshes its heartbeat; if the heartbeat is older than `heartbeat_timeout` (30 seconds by default), another worker can pick the job up again. On success the row is deleted from the queue and the outcome appended to `pgqueuer_log`. Workers also poll, so a missed notification only delays a job.

Because jobs are rows, a job can be enqueued in the same transaction as the data it’s about. PgQueuer adds cron-style schedules, deferred jobs (`execute_after`), retries with a delay, per-entrypoint concurrency limits enforced across all workers, deduplication keys, Prometheus metrics, a terminal dashboard and an in-memory mode for tests. It’s free under the MIT licence, needs Python 3.10+ and Postgres 14+, and reached 1.0 in May 2026 after two years of 0.x releases.
strengths: Transactional enqueue: the job commits or rolls back with your data, so there’s no dual write to drift
Jobs start right away through LISTEN/NOTIFY, with polling as a safety net
The usual job-queue features built in: cron schedules, deferred jobs, retries with backoff, cancellation, completion tracking and fleet-wide concurrency limits
Observability out of the box: Prometheus metrics, tracing with Logfire or Sentry, and `pgq dashboard`
Tests and prototypes can run without Postgres using `PgQueuer.in_memory()`
limits: Python only: handlers must be `async def`, and retries, cancellation and tracing are Python APIs, so workers in other languages aren’t an option
At least once: if a worker dies mid-job the job runs again, and a crash re-delivery doesn’t increase `attempts`, so handlers must be idempotent
Each finished job is a delete on a high-churn table; without the aggressive autovacuum settings from `pgq autovac`, dead tuples slow index scans
Claims, heartbeats and logs load the same Postgres instance as your application, and `pgqueuer_log` is never pruned automatically
No workflows: no chains, groups or DAGs, and nothing stores a handler’s return value

sections.title: pgmq, PgQue and PgQueuer
sections.intro: All three keep queues in Postgres tables. They differ in what a reader gets, which languages can join in, and how old rows are cleaned up.

rows.label: Model
values: Message queue: each message goes to one reader
Shared event log: every subscribed consumer sees every event
Job queue: Python workers run a handler per job

rows.label: What you install
values: SQL objects, as an extension or a plain SQL file
One PL/pgSQL file, plus a scheduler that calls the ticker
A Python package; `pgq install` creates its tables

rows.label: Languages
values: Any, through SQL; official Rust and Python clients
Any, through SQL; first-party Python, Go and TypeScript clients
Python 3.10+, async handlers

rows.label: Handing out work
values: `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, then a visibility timeout
Batches between ticks, found by comparing two transaction snapshots; no row locks
`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, then status `picked` with a heartbeat

rows.label: Delivery
values: Exactly once within the visibility timeout, then at least once
At least once, in batches; about 52 ms median wait at the default 100 ms tick
At least once; handlers must be idempotent

rows.label: Retries
values: The message reappears after the timeout; track `read_ct` yourself
`nack` schedules a retry; a dead-letter queue after the limit
`RetryRequested` with a delay, or hold failed jobs for review

rows.label: Finished messages
values: Deleted, or moved to an archive table
Stay in the log; `ack` moves the consumer’s cursor
Deleted from the queue; the outcome is appended to a log table

rows.label: Dead rows and cleanup
values: Updates and deletes leave dead rows for VACUUM; optional partitions dropped by pg_partman
None on the hot path: three tables rotate and the oldest is emptied with `TRUNCATE`
Deletes leave dead rows; `pgq autovac` makes autovacuum aggressive

notes: PgQue’s latency figure comes from its own committed benchmark.

story: Celery, a long-standing Python job queue, runs beside a separate broker such as Redis, RabbitMQ or SQS, plus a `celery-beat` process for recurring tasks. Yet Postgres already has what a queue needs: row locks with `SKIP LOCKED`, so workers don’t collide, and LISTEN/NOTIFY to wake them. In April 2024 a developer who publishes on GitHub as janbjorge (JeyBee) released PgQueuer to use just those, so an application that already has Postgres needs no other broker.

Early Show HN posts in April and May 2024 advertised over 5,000 jobs a second, and a post that August drew 376 points. Features arrived in quick 0.x releases, such as recurring schedules in 0.15 (November 2024) and deduplication keys in 0.20 (April 2025).

After about two years and 26 minor releases, 1.0 shipped on 11 May 2026 as the first stable release, with strict semantic versioning from then on. The project records its design in architecture decision records: workers claim jobs by lock contention, notifications only signal and never carry job data, and delivery is at least once.

choices.choice: Workers race for rows; no coordinator assigns work
choices.why: With `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, any worker can claim any ready job and the database arbitrates, so there’s no coordinator or worker registry to run. The cost is no fairness between workers and lock traffic at the head of the queue.

choices.choice: NOTIFY wakes workers but never carries the job
choices.why: NOTIFY payloads are capped at about 8 kB, vanish if the sending transaction rolls back, and are missed by late listeners. So a wake-up only prompts a normal claim query, and a periodic poll covers anything missed.
Exactly-once would need fencing tokens or an outbox and still breaks once side effects leave the database. Re-running a crashed job was judged better than losing it.
